Every one of those platforms can change its algorithm, suspend your account, or decide creators are worth less reach next quarter, and there is nothing you can do about it. The one thing that stays yours no matter what a platform does is a site with your name on it. Most creators skip this because the obvious alternative, a link-in-bio tool, solves the wrong problem: it gets your links in one place, but it looks exactly like every other link-in-bio page, because it is the same template with your photo dropped in.

You describe the site you want in plain English, and it generates an actual Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS v4 application: real component files, not a locked-down mockup. One click publishes the site to a public URL at yourname.kodely.site , free, included, no separate hosting purchase, and every publish is scanned for accidentally-leaked API keys before it goes live.

41	So the output Kodely publishes is static in the hosting sense described above: pre-built files served as-is, not regenerated per visitor by a server. That's exactly why it's fast and simple to host, and why every publish gets scanned for leaked secrets before going live — there's a small, well-defined set of files to check, not a live application with a database behind it. 
42	Being static-served doesn't mean the site is inert, though. React adds real interactivity in the browser after the page loads — animations, state, interactive components all work fine. That's the direct consequence of the architecture, not a missing checkbox — there's no server component to do that per-request computation on. Editing is chat-based (describe the change, Kodely updates the real components), every generation is a free checkpoint you can roll back to, and you can view and copy the generated source in-app, though there's no zip export yet.

44	Related terms 
45	Static site generator (SSG): a tool that compiles source files into a static HTML/CSS/JS bundle ahead of time. 
46	Server-side rendering (SSR): generating HTML on the server for each request, often to support dynamic or personalized content. 
47	Client-side rendering (CSR): JavaScript in the browser builds or updates the page after the initial static files load — this is how a static-served React app gets its interactivity.

17	Be honest about donations 
18	One thing Kodely will not do: process an actual donation. Ask it to build a Donate button or a donation section, and it will - a clear, well-placed call to action styled to match the rest of your site. But Kodely generates frontend code only. It does not build a backend, a database, or a payment integration. To actually accept money, you connect that Donate button to a real payment processor as a separate step - a Stripe donation link, or a platform built for nonprofits such as Donorbox. That is normal: most nonprofit sites, however they are built, lean on a dedicated donation platform rather than custom payment code, and it is worth budgeting a small amount of time to wire that connection up once your site is live. 
19	Pricing in plain terms

8	The problem: no time, no budget, and the DIY options do not fit 
9	You run a small business. You are not short on things to do — you are short on the one thing a website takes: uninterrupted hours to learn a tool, write copy, and fight with a layout. Hiring a developer or an agency to build a simple site can run well past a thousand dollars and take weeks of back-and-forth. That is a lot to spend before you have proof the site brings in a single customer. 
10	So most owners try a do-it-yourself builder instead. The cheap ones produce sites that look like every other cheap site — the same templates, the same stock layout, nothing that says this business is real and run by someone who cares. The more capable ones ask you to learn a drag-and-drop editor that eats an entire weekend before you have a homepage you are willing to share. Either way, you end up with something that took too long or looks like it did not. 
11	How Kodely fits 
12	Kodely skips both problems. You describe your business in plain English in a chat interface — what you do, who you serve, what you want on the page. Kodely generates a real application from that description: a Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS v4 project made of actual component files, not a static mockup or a page of raw HTML. You watch a live preview render the real compiled app as it is built, so you are looking at the actual site, not an approximation of it. 
13	When it looks right, one click publishes it to a real public URL at your own <name>.kodely.site address, free, included in every plan. Need to change something later? Describe the change in chat and Kodely edits the real components behind the scenes. Every successful generation is saved as a checkpoint, so if a change goes sideways, rolling back costs nothing. And if you want to see exactly what was built, the code view shows you the actual generated source files, in-app, that you can read and copy. 
14	Three businesses this is built for 
15	A local service business 
16	A plumber, an electrician, a cleaning company, a landscaper. What these sites need is not complicated: hours, service area, a list of what you offer, a phone number that is easy to find, and something that signals a real, established business when someone searches your name after getting a referral. Describe the services and the service area in chat, and Kodely builds exactly that. 
17	A small shop 
18	A boutique, a bakery, a bike shop — a business where the website's job is to answer where are you, when are you open, and what do you carry, then get the visitor to walk in or call. An informational site that looks intentional does that job well, and it is exactly what Kodely is built to produce fast. 
19	A one-person consultancy 
20	Freelancers and independent consultants often put off having a website entirely because a portfolio site feels like a project of its own. Describing your services, your background, and how to reach you in chat gets you a page that looks like you took your business seriously — because a credible site is often the difference between a prospect emailing you and moving on to the next search result. 
21	What Kodely is honest about not doing yet 
22	Kodely builds the front end of your site — the pages, the layout, the content, the design. It does not generate a backend, a database, user accounts, or payment processing, so if your business needs online ordering or an appointment-booking system built into the site, that is not what Kodely does today. Sites also publish to a *.kodely.site subdomain rather than a custom domain, and editing happens through chat rather than a click-to-edit visual canvas. For a professional informational site — the kind most small businesses actually need first — none of that gets in the way. It matters if you were expecting a full ordering or booking platform out of the box. 
23	Pricing, in plain terms

20	A real example 
21	Say someone wants a landing page for a new pottery studio. In a vibe coding workflow, they don't open a code editor or pick a template. They type something like: "Build me a one-page site for a pottery studio called Clayworks — hero section with a class-signup button, a section showing our three class types, and a contact section with our studio address." The AI generates the actual page: real components, real layout, real styling. The person looks at it rendered live, then says "make the hero darker and move the class types above the fold" — and the AI updates the real code behind the page to match. No line of code was hand-typed by the person, but a working, structured site came out the other end. 
22	How Kodely applies vibe coding to websites

11	Traditional website builders 
12	You start from a template or a blank canvas, then drag sections, text blocks, images, and buttons into place. The builder stores your design as data inside its own platform — there's no file you can open in a code editor, because there isn't really a codebase in the conventional sense. Changes happen by clicking and dragging, not describing. This is why these tools have historically been the easiest entry point for non-technical users: what you see in the editor is what visitors see, with no code involved anywhere.
